It may claim cessation of continuing wrongs and full reparation, including compensation for the deaths (Chorzów Factory, 1928; Arts 31-36).

Conclusion: Tolan can hold Mirela responsible both for its police's omission and, under Art 10, for the Front's attack. Sarvia is responsible for its officers' conduct and, if they controlled the operation, for the attack itself.

questions.q: The fictional State of Karst has suffered repeated rocket attacks over two years from the 'Northern Brigade', an armed group based in the territory of State Lumen. The latest attack killed 40 Karst civilians. Lumen's government condemns the Brigade but lacks the military capacity to remove it. Karst, without Security Council authorisation or Lumen's consent, launches air strikes against Brigade camps inside Lumen, also destroying a Lumen army depot it says was supplying the Brigade. Karst reports the strikes to the Security Council. Advise on the legality of Karst's action.
markScheme: Art 2(4) prohibition; strikes on Lumen's territory are use of force against it regardless of target.
No Security Council authorisation or consent; self-defence is the only possible justification.
Armed attack: gravity threshold (Nicaragua); accumulation of events doctrine for repeated attacks.
Attacks by non-state actors: Art 51 text; Wall (2004) and Armed Activities (2005) positions; post-9/11 Resolutions 1368 and 1373.
Attribution to Lumen: not established (effective control); Lumen condemns the Brigade.
'Unwilling or unable' doctrine: support and opposition; Lumen is unable.
Necessity: imminence of further attacks; whether peaceful alternatives were exhausted.
Proportionality: strikes on camps vs destruction of a Lumen army depot without proof of state involvement.
Reporting requirement under Art 51 satisfied; not determinative (Nicaragua).
Notes possible IHL issues if civilians harmed.
Reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The strikes are uses of force on Lumen's territory and engage Art 2(4) of the UN Charter, even though they target a non-state group. Without Security Council authorisation or Lumen's consent, Karst can rely only on self-defence under Art 51.

Armed attack. Rocket attacks killing 40 civilians, part of a two-year campaign, are grave enough to meet the threshold in Nicaragua (1986). The accumulation of events doctrine, which the ICJ has entertained (Oil Platforms, 2003), supports treating the series as one armed attack.

Non-state actors. Art 51 does not say who must carry out the armed attack, but in the Wall Advisory Opinion (2004) the ICJ linked self-defence to attacks by states, and in Armed Activities (2005) it found it unnecessary to decide the point. The Brigade's conduct is not attributable to Lumen under the effective control test (Nicaragua; Bosnia Genocide), especially as Lumen condemns it. Karst must therefore rely on the view that self-defence is available against non-state actors. Security Council Resolutions 1368 and 1373 (2001) support this view, and states such as the US and UK have relied on an 'unwilling or unable' test, which Lumen's incapacity would satisfy. Many states and scholars reject this test as a dangerous expansion. The legality of the strikes on the camps is therefore arguable but contested.

Necessity and proportionality. Repeated attacks suggest more are imminent, supporting necessity. Strikes limited to Brigade camps could be proportionate to stopping the attacks. The destruction of Lumen's army depot is far harder to defend. It targets the territorial state itself, and Karst merely asserts that the depot supplied the Brigade. Unless it can prove Lumen's support amounted to its own armed attack or that the depot was being used by the Brigade, striking state military assets exceeds what is needed to repel the non-state threat.

Karst's report to the Security Council satisfies Art 51's procedural requirement.

Conclusion: strikes on Brigade camps may be defensible on the contested 'unable' theory, but the attack on Lumen's depot is likely an unlawful use of force engaging Karst's responsibility.

questions.q: 'The UN Charter's system for controlling the use of force has failed, and international law should now recognise a right of unilateral humanitarian intervention.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains the Charter scheme: Art 2(4), Chapter VII, Art 51; jus cogens status.
Assesses the Security Council's record: Cold War paralysis, the 1990s, the veto (Rwanda, Syria, Ukraine).
Discusses arguments for humanitarian intervention: Art 2(4) narrow reading, moral necessity, Kosovo (1999), UK Syria positions (2013, 2018).
UK's criteria: convincing evidence of extreme distress, no practicable alternative, necessity and proportionality.

Arguments against: weak state practice and opinio juris; G77 rejection; ICJ in Nicaragua rejecting forcible intervention for human rights; risk of abuse (e.g. Russia's genocide claims re Ukraine 2022).
Responsibility to Protect: World Summit Outcome 2005 channels force through the Council; Libya 2011 and its aftermath.
Alternatives: Uniting for Peace, regional organisations (AU Constitutive Act Art 4(h)), veto restraint initiatives.
Considers Ukraine v Russia (Allegations of Genocide) provisional measures (2022).
Discusses jus cogens: whether a new exception could form.
Reasoned conclusion engaging with both legal and policy dimensions.
questions.modelAnswer:
The Charter prohibits the threat or use of force (Art 2(4)) except under Security Council authorisation (Chapter VII) or self-defence (Art 51). The prohibition is customary and widely regarded as jus cogens. The system relies on the Council acting when atrocities occur, and the veto often prevents this: the Council failed in Rwanda in 1994, and Russia and China blocked action on Syria repeatedly after 2011.

Supporters of humanitarian intervention argue that Art 2(4) bans only force against territorial integrity or political independence, so a limited rescue operation does not breach it. They point to NATO's Kosovo campaign (1999) and to the UK's legal positions on Syria (2013 and 2018), which asserted a right to intervene where there is convincing evidence of extreme humanitarian distress, no practicable alternative, and force that is necessary and proportionate.

The legal case is weak. The narrow reading of Art 2(4) was rejected in Corfu Channel (1949), and Nicaragua held that force is not an appropriate method to ensure respect for human rights. State practice is thin and opinio juris weaker still: the Kosovo intervention was justified mainly in political terms, and the Group of 77, representing over 130 states, rejected any so-called right of humanitarian intervention in 2000. Modifying a jus cogens norm requires acceptance by the international community as a whole (Art 53 VCLT), which is absent.

There is also a risk of abuse. Russia justified its 2022 invasion of Ukraine partly by alleging genocide in eastern Ukraine; the ICJ ordered Russia to suspend its military operations (2022).

The Responsibility to Protect (World Summit Outcome, 2005) offers a compromise: states must protect their populations, and the international community may take collective action through the Council. Libya (2011) showed its potential and, as the operation drifted towards regime change, its dangers. Other routes include Uniting for Peace, Art 4(h) of the African Union Constitutive Act, and veto restraint initiatives.

The Charter system is imperfect but has not collapsed. A unilateral right would probably cause more harm than it prevents. Reform should focus on making collective mechanisms work rather than weakening the prohibition on force.

questions.q: The fictional State of Nordia, a party to the ICCPR and its First Optional Protocol, faces a wave of terrorist attacks. It declares a state of emergency and passes a law allowing indefinite detention without trial of foreign nationals suspected of terrorism, while citizens suspected of terrorism remain subject to ordinary criminal law. Nordia also runs a detention facility on an island it leases from a neighbouring state, where it holds suspects captured abroad, and its interrogators there use sleep deprivation and stress positions. Advise on Nordia's compliance with international human rights law.
markScheme: Right to liberty (Art 9 ICCPR) engaged by indefinite detention without trial.
Derogation under Art 4 ICCPR: public emergency threatening life of the nation; official proclamation; notification to the UN Secretary-General.
Strictly required test; deference to state's assessment but review of proportionality.
Non-discrimination: Art 4(1) prohibits derogations that discriminate solely on listed grounds; also Art 26; A v Home Secretary (2004) reasoning on targeting foreigners.
Extraterritorial jurisdiction: leased island under Nordia's effective control; Art 2(1) 'within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction' read disjunctively (General Comment 31; Wall).
Personal control over detainees (Al-Skeini analogy; Lopez Burgos v Uruguay).
Torture/ill-treatment prohibition (Art 7 ICCPR; CAT): non-derogable (Art 4(2)) and jus cogens.

Classification of sleep deprivation and stress positions: Ireland v UK (1978), its 2018 revision refusal; Human Rights Committee and CAT views treat such techniques as prohibited; at least cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.
Remedies: individual communications under the Optional Protocol, state reporting, effective remedy (Art 2(3)).
Clear conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Detention. Indefinite detention without trial engages the right to liberty under Art 9 ICCPR, which forbids arbitrary detention and guarantees prompt review by a court. Nordia can justify the scheme only by derogating under Art 4.

Derogation requires a public emergency threatening the life of the nation, officially proclaimed, and notified to the other parties through the UN Secretary-General. A wave of terrorist attacks may qualify. But measures must be strictly required by the exigencies of the situation, and Art 4(1) forbids derogations that are inconsistent with other international obligations or that discriminate solely on the ground of race, colour, sex, language, religion or social origin. Nationality is not on that list, but differential treatment of foreigners must still be strictly required and consistent with Arts 2(1) and 26. In A v Home Secretary (2004) the House of Lords found the UK's equivalent scheme disproportionate and discriminatory for exactly this reason: if citizen suspects could be managed under ordinary law, detaining only foreigners was not strictly required. Nordia's scheme is likely unlawful.

The island facility. Art 2(1) ICCPR applies to individuals within a state's territory and subject to its jurisdiction. The Human Rights Committee (General Comment 31, 2004) and the ICJ (Wall, 2004) read this as covering anyone within a state's power or effective control, even abroad (see Lopez Burgos v Uruguay, 1981). Nordia controls the leased island and holds the detainees, so its obligations apply there; the European Court reached the same result in Al-Skeini (2011).

Interrogation. Art 7 ICCPR prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and Art 4(2) makes it non-derogable. The prohibition of torture is jus cogens. In Ireland v UK (1978) the European Court classified the five techniques, including stress positions and sleep deprivation, as inhuman and degrading treatment rather than torture, and refused to revise that classification in 2018. Treaty bodies such as the Committee against Torture have treated such techniques as capable of amounting to torture, especially when combined or prolonged. Either way they are absolutely prohibited.

Detainees may bring individual communications under the First Optional Protocol, and Nordia must provide an effective remedy (Art 2(3)).

Conclusion: the discriminatory detention scheme, and the treatment on the island, breach the ICCPR.

questions.q: The fictional States of Arden and Bellmont have both made declarations under Art 36(2) of the ICJ Statute. Arden's declaration excludes 'disputes relating to matters which are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of Arden as determined by Arden'. Bellmont's declaration excludes disputes concerning its territorial waters. Arden's navy seizes a Bellmont fishing vessel in waters Bellmont claims as its territorial sea; Arden calls this an internal law enforcement matter. Both states are also parties to a fisheries treaty with a compromissory clause referring disputes to the ICJ. Bellmont wants to sue Arden and to obtain the release of the crew urgently. Advise Bellmont.
markScheme: Explains consent basis of contentious jurisdiction (Art 36) and optional clause reciprocity.
Arden's self-judging (automatic) reservation: validity contested (Judge Lauterpacht in Norwegian Loans), but likely to be invoked.
Reciprocity: Arden can rely on Bellmont's territorial waters reservation (Norwegian Loans) since dispute concerns waters Bellmont claims.
Consideration of how the Court characterises the dispute (Fisheries Jurisdiction (Spain v Canada), 1998).
Compromissory clause as an independent basis; dispute must fall within the treaty's subject-matter.
Requirements such as prior negotiation conditions in the clause (Georgia v Russia, 2011).
Provisional measures: prima facie jurisdiction, plausibility, link, urgency/irreparable harm (Art 41; LaGrand binding).
Alternative forums: UNCLOS prompt release under Art 292 before ITLOS if both are parties.
Clear advice.
questions.modelAnswer:
Optional clause. Under Art 36(2) of the ICJ Statute, jurisdiction exists only to the extent the two declarations overlap, and each state may rely on the other's reservations by reciprocity (Norwegian Loans, 1957). Arden's self-judging domestic jurisdiction reservation lets it decide for itself that the dispute is domestic. Judge Lauterpacht argued in Norwegian Loans that such reservations are invalid because they contradict Art 36(6), under which the Court decides its own jurisdiction, but the Court has never ruled on the point and Arden will invoke it.

More seriously, Bellmont's own reservation excludes disputes concerning its territorial waters, and Arden can rely on it by reciprocity. Since Bellmont alleges the seizure occurred in its territorial sea, the dispute seems to fall within that exclusion. In Fisheries Jurisdiction (Spain v Canada) (1998) the Court interpreted reservations naturally in light of the declaring state's intention. The optional clause route therefore looks weak.

Compromissory clause. The fisheries treaty provides an independent basis of jurisdiction under Art 36(1), unaffected by the optional clause reservations. Bellmont must show the dispute concerns the treaty's interpretation or application, for example its rules on fishing rights or enforcement. Any preconditions in the clause, such as negotiation, must be satisfied: in Georgia v Russia (2011) the Court declined jurisdiction because Georgia had not genuinely attempted negotiation.

Provisional measures. Bellmont can seek an order for the crew's release under Art 41. It must show prima facie jurisdiction, which the compromissory clause may provide, plausible rights under the treaty, a link between those rights and release, and urgency with a risk of irreparable harm, which detention of crew may satisfy. Orders are binding (LaGrand, 2001).

Alternative. If both states are parties to UNCLOS, Art 292 allows a prompt release application to ITLOS on posting of a reasonable bond, where the detention concerns fisheries enforcement in the EEZ; this may be quicker.

Advice: rely on the compromissory clause, satisfy any preconditions, and seek provisional measures or an ITLOS prompt release order.

questions.q: 'The International Court of Justice's dependence on state consent makes it a weak institution, but that very weakness is the source of its authority.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains the consent basis (Art 36) and its forms.
Notes the limited acceptance of the optional clause (fewer than half of UN members), withdrawals (US after Nicaragua, 1985) and reservations.
Discusses Monetary Gold and East Timor as consent-based limits.
Compliance record: generally good, but notable failures (Nicaragua; LaGrand; Avena; Ukraine v Russia provisional measures).
Art 94(2) enforcement limited by veto.
Growth of compromissory-clause cases and erga omnes partes standing (Belgium v Senegal; Gambia v Myanmar; South Africa v Israel).
Advisory opinions as an expanding role (Chagos, 2019; occupied Palestinian territory, 2024; climate change, 2025) and the consent debate.
Arguments that consent underpins legitimacy, compliance and perceived impartiality.
Counter-arguments: weakness undermines rule of law; selective acceptance favours powerful states.
Comparison with compulsory systems (WTO's crisis; ITLOS/UNCLOS Part XV).
Reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The ICJ decides contentious cases only with the consent of the states involved (Art 36 Statute). Consent may be given by special agreement, by compromissory clauses or by optional clause declarations, but fewer than half of UN members accept the optional clause, often with broad reservations. The US withdrew its declaration in 1985, after losing the jurisdiction phase of Nicaragua (1984). Enforcement under Art 94(2) depends on a Security Council where a permanent member can block action.

These limits produce visible failures. The US ignored Nicaragua; it also failed to stop the execution of German nationals in LaGrand despite a provisional measures order. Russia did not comply with the 2022 order to suspend military operations in Ukraine.

Yet the Court's docket has grown. Compromissory clauses in multilateral treaties, combined with standing based on obligations erga omnes partes, have allowed states with no direct injury to sue: Belgium v Senegal (2012), Gambia v Myanmar (2022) and South Africa v Israel (2024). Advisory jurisdiction has also expanded. Chagos (2019), the 2024 opinion on Israel's policies in the occupied Palestinian territory, and the 2025 climate change opinion address issues where contentious jurisdiction would be unavailable, though critics say this sidesteps consent.

The argument that weakness creates authority runs as follows. Because states consent, they are more likely to comply, and most judgments, especially boundary cases under special agreements, have been implemented. The Court's caution in delimiting its jurisdiction protects its reputation for impartiality and keeps states engaged. A court with compulsory jurisdiction and no enforcement might simply be ignored. The WTO, where the US blocked Appellate Body appointments citing overreach, shows how a stronger body can provoke backlash.

The argument has limits. Consent-based jurisdiction lets powerful states avoid adjudication, which undermines equality before the law. Recent expansions show its authority also comes from a public, community function.

The best view is that consent is a foundation rather than a weakness. The Court's authority rests on legal reasoning and careful respect for its limits, which allows it to build jurisdiction gradually without provoking the withdrawals that would truly weaken it.

questions.q: Explain how a norm acquires jus cogens status and the legal consequences of that status.
markScheme: Art 53 VCLT: a norm accepted and recognised by the international community of states as a whole as one from which no derogation is permitted.
Identification requires a norm of general international law plus acceptance of its non-derogable character by a very large majority of states (ILC Conclusions on peremptory norms, 2022).
Treaties conflicting with jus cogens are void (Art 53) or become void when a new norm emerges (Art 64).
No circumstance precluding wrongfulness justifies breach (Art 26 ARSIWA); serious breaches trigger non-recognition and cooperation duties (Arts 40-41).
Limits: jus cogens does not override procedural rules such as state immunity (Germany v Italy, 2012) or ICJ consent (Armed Activities (DRC v Rwanda), 2006).
questions.modelAnswer: Under Art 53 VCLT, a peremptory norm is accepted by the international community of states as a whole as one from which no derogation is permitted. The ILC's 2022 Conclusions require a norm of general international law whose non-derogable character a very large majority of states accept. Consequences: a conflicting treaty is void (Art 53), or becomes void if the norm emerges later (Art 64); no circumstance precluding wrongfulness can justify a breach (Art 26 ARSIWA); and serious breaches oblige all states not to recognise the resulting situation (Art 41). But it does not override procedural rules such as state immunity (Germany v Italy, 2012) or consent to ICJ jurisdiction (Armed Activities (DRC v Rwanda), 2006).

questions.q: Identify the main bases on which a state may assert criminal jurisdiction over conduct occurring outside its territory.
markScheme: Nationality (active personality): offences committed abroad by its nationals.
Passive personality and the protective principle: offences against its nationals abroad, or conduct threatening its security or governmental functions (e.g. counterfeiting).
Universality: crimes such as piracy, genocide, war crimes and torture, regardless of where committed or by whom.
questions.modelAnswer: Territoriality is the primary basis of jurisdiction, but states may also legislate for conduct abroad in recognised cases. Under the nationality principle a state may prosecute its own nationals for offences committed abroad. The passive personality principle covers offences against its nationals abroad and is increasingly accepted for terrorism. The protective principle covers conduct threatening the state's security or governmental functions, such as counterfeiting its currency. Universal jurisdiction allows any state to prosecute certain grave crimes, including piracy, genocide, war crimes and torture, wherever they occur and whoever commits them.

questions.q: 'Immunity is procedural and jus cogens is substantive, so the two never conflict.' Critically assess this reasoning as a basis for upholding immunity in cases involving serious violations of international law.
markScheme: Explains the procedural/substantive distinction as used in Germany v Italy (2012) and Arrest Warrant (2002).
Sets out the jus cogens argument: hierarchy of norms means immunity must yield (Ferrini, Italian Court of Cassation, 2004; Al-Adsani dissent).
Analyses Al-Adsani v UK (2001) and Jones v UK (2014) under Art 6 ECHR.
Analyses Jones v Saudi Arabia (House of Lords, 2006) on officials in civil claims.
Contrasts criminal immunity ratione materiae: Pinochet (No 3) (1999) and its Torture Convention reasoning.
Discusses Arrest Warrant's assurance that immunity is not impunity, and its four routes.
Considers draft Art 7 of the ILC's draft articles on immunity of state officials (first reading, 2022) and state divisions over it.
Considers Italian Constitutional Court judgment 238/2014 and subsequent Germany v Italy (II) proceedings.
Evaluates the coherence of the distinction: whether procedural bars can effectively deny substantive rights (access to court).
Policy considerations: inter-state relations, floodgates, sovereign equality vs accountability.
Reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The reasoning comes most clearly from Germany v Italy (2012). Italian courts, following Ferrini (2004), had denied Germany immunity for wartime atrocities, arguing that jus cogens must prevail over immunity. The ICJ disagreed. Immunity, it said, is a procedural rule determining whether a court may exercise jurisdiction; it does not address whether the conduct was lawful. So the two rules operate on different planes and cannot conflict. Arrest Warrant (2002) used similar logic, stressing that immunity does not mean impunity.

The European Court of Human Rights reached comparable results under Art 6 ECHR. In Al-Adsani v UK (2001), by nine votes to eight, it held that granting Kuwait immunity in a civil torture claim was a proportionate restriction on access to court. Jones v UK (2014) extended this to officials (following Jones v Saudi Arabia, HL 2006).

The distinction has force. Immunity reflects sovereign equality, and removing it in civil cases could expose states to litigation over historical wrongs in many forums, damaging inter-state relations.

But the reasoning is open to criticism. A procedural rule that blocks every forum effectively denies the substantive right, as the Al-Adsani dissenters argued. The distinction is also applied inconsistently. In Pinochet (No 3) (1999) the House of Lords denied immunity ratione materiae for torture in criminal proceedings, reasoning that the Torture Convention could not coherently define torture as official conduct and then shield it as an official act. Draft Art 7 of the ILC's draft articles on immunity of state officials (first reading, 2022) excludes immunity ratione materiae for crimes including genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and torture, though states are divided on whether this reflects existing law. The Italian Constitutional Court (judgment 238/2014) refused to give the ICJ ruling domestic effect.

The procedural-substantive distinction is formally coherent but morally thin. It best explains the civil immunity of states and the personal immunity of serving senior officials, where strong interests in stability apply. It is less persuasive for the functional immunity of former officials in criminal cases, where developing practice suggests that serious international crimes cannot be treated as protected official acts.
